6.6 The Household Balance Sheet and Insurance

This content was generated by AI. It may contain errors and is not investment advice.

All lessons, questions and reference answers on this site were generated by AI and have not been reviewed by a professional. Their correctness is not guaranteed. If you find an error, please report it with the link at the bottom of the page. The content is for learning only and is not investment advice.

The investment portfolio is only one part of a household’s finances. Before deciding on a stock share, look at all of the household’s assets and liabilities, and at the risks that the portfolio cannot, and should not, carry.

The household balance sheet

Section titled “The household balance sheet”

The household balance sheet lists a household’s assets and liabilities: financial assets (cash, taxable accounts, retirement accounts), real assets such as a home, and liabilities such as the mortgage, car loans, student loans and credit cards; the difference is net worth.

For a household of working age, the largest asset is usually not in any account but is human capital (human capital): the present value of future earnings. Human capital cannot be sold or diversified; its risk depends on how secure the job is and how closely earnings move with the stock market and with the employer’s stock (4.12 Life-Cycle Asset Allocation Theory). Many household financial decisions are really about protecting or supplementing human capital.

Check C1
Following the pattern in Figure 1-1, how does a primary earner with children usually need life insurance coverage to change with age?
The probability of death affects the premium, but what should the coverage protect? How does that part of wealth change with age in the figure?
Once the children are grown, for how many more years does the family need the income? How much can the financial assets already saved cover?

The emergency fund

Section titled “The emergency fund”

An emergency fund is money set aside for job loss, illness or unexpected expenses, available at any time and stable in value, usually held in a high-yield savings account, a money market fund or short-term Treasuries. A common guideline is 3 to 6 months of essential expenses; households with unsteady income, a single earner or high layoff risk in their industry need more.

The emergency fund lets a household avoid selling investments at a bad time or borrowing on high-rate credit cards when something goes wrong. Its return is low, which can be seen as the insurance premium for this protection.

Check C2
An emergency fund is better kept in a stock index fund, because stocks earn more in the long run and can be sold any time when needed.
When is a household most likely to need its emergency fund? What state is the stock market usually in then?

Managing debt

Section titled “Managing debt”

Interest rates on debts differ widely. Credit card rates are often above 20%; almost no investment can reliably beat that, so such debt should be paid off first. For a lower-rate mortgage, a common question is whether spare money should go to prepaying the mortgage or to investing.

Prepaying 1 dollar of the mortgage saves the interest on that dollar from then on, which amounts to a return equal to the mortgage rate, with no risk. If mortgage interest is not itemized (the 2026 standard deduction for married couples filing jointly is 32,200 dollars, and many households no longer itemize), this is also the after-tax return (Exercises Question 1).

Check C3
A household with no emergency fund plans to put all its savings into prepaying its 6% mortgage. The main drawback is:
Prepaying 1 dollar saves how much interest from then on? The return itself is not low. The problem lies elsewhere.
Does the house's value depend on the loan balance? What does prepaying change?

Insurance

Section titled “Insurance”

Insurance swaps a possible large loss for a certain small payment. For a risk-averse person this can be worthwhile even when the premium exceeds the expected loss (1.4 Choice Under Uncertainty). But insurers have costs and need a profit, so premiums are on average higher than expected payouts; insurance therefore suits rare but large losses that one could not afford, while small losses are better borne oneself, for example by choosing higher deductibles.

The kinds of insurance households most often need:

  • Term life insurance: if the insured person dies within the agreed term (say 20 years), the insurer pays the face amount. It protects the part of human capital the family depends on, at a premium far below that of whole life insurance, which combines insurance with savings.
  • Disability insurance: if illness or injury prevents work, it pays part of the income each month, usually around 60%. The US Social Security Administration estimates that more than one in four of today’s 20-year-olds will become disabled before reaching retirement age.
  • Umbrella insurance adds, on top of the liability limits of car and home insurance, further liability coverage of, for example, 1 million dollars, protecting against losing most of one’s property in a lawsuit.
  • Health insurance, home and car insurance, and insurance for long-term care.
Check C4
Among the following, by the principle of "rare but large losses one could not afford", which is least worth buying for a young two-income household?
If one person could not work for decades, how large would the loss be? Could the household bear it alone?
A lawsuit for hundreds of thousands of dollars is unlikely, but if it happened, could the household pay? Is such insurance usually expensive?

Estate planning

Section titled “Estate planning”

Estate planning decides who receives property and decision-making power when a family member dies or can no longer act:

  • A will names how property is divided and who becomes guardian of minor children.
  • A beneficiary designation: retirement accounts, life insurance and similar assets can name beneficiaries directly; on the owner’s death they pass straight to the beneficiaries without going through probate.
  • A revocable living trust: assets are placed in a trust with oneself as trustee; on death they are distributed according to the trust document, also without probate and without being made public.
  • Powers of attorney and health care directives name who handles finances and makes medical decisions if one cannot.

Federal estate tax concerns only very large estates: under the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the exemption is 15 million dollars per person in 2026, adjusted for inflation afterwards; some states have their own estate taxes with much lower thresholds.

Check C5
A man who divorced and remarried wrote a new will leaving everything to his current wife, but his 401(k) still names his former wife as beneficiary. After his death, the 401(k) goes to his current wife according to the will.
How does an account with a named beneficiary pass on the owner's death? Does it go through probate?

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • The household balance sheet includes financial assets, real assets, liabilities, and the largest asset, human capital.
  • The emergency fund holds 3 to 6 months or more of essential expenses, somewhere stable and always available.
  • Pay off high-rate debt first; prepaying a mortgage earns a riskless return equal to the mortgage rate.
  • Insurance suits rare but large losses; term life and disability insurance protect human capital, and umbrella insurance protects property from liability claims.
  • Wills, beneficiary designations, trusts and powers of attorney decide where property and decisions go.

Exercises

Section titled “Exercises”
Question 1
A couple has a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage at 2.9% (taken out in 2021) and does not itemize. They have 60,000 dollars in cash, 40,000 of which is their emergency fund. Short-term Treasury bills now yield 4.0%, Treasury interest is exempt from state tax, and their federal marginal tax rate is 24%.
(a) What is the after-tax yield on cash held in Treasury bills? By how much does it exceed the mortgage rate?
(b) They say: "Having no debt is safest. We should use all 60,000 dollars to prepay the mortgage." Evaluate this statement. How would your advice change if the mortgage rate were 7%?
Question 2
A 35-year-old primary earner has two young children. If he dies, the family needs 90,000 dollars a year (in today's purchasing power) for the next 20 years for living and education costs, after which the children are independent. The real discount rate is 2%, and each year's need is paid at year end. The household has 300,000 dollars of usable financial assets.
(a) What is the present value of the family's 20 years of needs? Roughly what is the life insurance gap (thousand dollars)?
(b) An insurance salesperson recommends 1.5 million dollars of whole life insurance, because "with term insurance the money is wasted if you outlive it, while whole life both protects and saves, for your whole life". Evaluate this recommendation.
Question 3
A 30-year-old engineer earns 200,000 dollars a year before tax, expected to grow 2% a year in real terms, and plans to work until 65 (35 years); the real discount rate is 3%. He has 150,000 dollars of financial assets and no disability insurance.
(a) Treating the first year's income as 200,000 dollars received at year end, estimate his human capital with the growing annuity formula (thousand dollars). What percentage of his total wealth is human capital?
(b) He says: "I'm young and healthy, so disability insurance is a waste of money; my biggest risk is a stock market fall, so I hold only 60% stocks." Evaluate this statement.
Question 4
A couple both work at the same technology company and have essential expenses of 10,000 dollars a month. In an industry downturn they estimate they might both lose their jobs, and finding new jobs could take up to 9 months; while unemployed they would together receive about 4,000 dollars a month in unemployment benefits, for at most 6 months.
(a) At a minimum, how large must the emergency fund be to cover this case (thousand dollars)?
(b) Their adviser suggests the generic rule of 3 months of expenses (30,000 dollars), with everything else in company stock and technology funds, because "you know this industry". Evaluate this advice.
